newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-State election looms for Western Australia.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-State election looms for Western Australia.

text.p: The big question mark hanging over the next election in Western Australia appears to be not who will govern for the next four years but the date of the poll.
There is an outside chance the 106-year conservative reign in the upper house - the Legislative Council - may finally come to an end.

However, opinion polls and pundits alike are predicting the Liberal Party/National Party Coalition will retain control of the all-important lower house - the Legislative Assembly - either in its own right or in some loose confederation with conservative-minded independents.

The date of the poll is harder to predict. Traditionally the state election is held in February or March but an early election is being strongly tipped by sources in both major parties, with speculation centering on December 14.
An early poll would give the ALP's new leader, Dr Geoff Gallop, only a matter of weeks to make his presence felt.

But one well-placed political observer suggested the leadership change may actually tip the balance in favour of a post-Christmas election because of a view within Coalition ranks that the longer Gallop has on the hustings the less attractive he will prove to the electors.
Gallop swapped jobs in October with the then leader Jim McGinty mainly because of the latter's poor showing in opinion polls. Even so, he is not expected to lead the party to victory.
"The best we can hope for (in the Legislative Assembly) is to hold onto the furniture (not lose any seats)," said one senior Labor Party source who asked not to be named.
The 57-seat Assembly is currently occupied by 32 Coalition MPs, 22 Labor and 3 Independent, two of whom are former members of the Liberal Party and one a former Labor MP.
Each represents a single district and is elected by preferential voting, a system that traditionally favours the major parties.

Despite a redistribution in 1994 the ALP could win with only 47.5 percent of the vote. Based on the 1993 election results, it only needs a two-per-cent swing to reach that target and, post redistribution, there are six Coalition seats (versus only 2 ALP) vulnerable to a swing of two-per-cent or less.

Over the past 12 months Labor has managed to shore up one of its main policy weaknesses (in relation to law and order) while also taking full toll of government stumbling in education, health and industrial relations.
So why the pessimism in ALP ranks?
Firstly, tradition: WA voters rarely throw out a government afte just one term.
Secondly: Labor continues to show up poorly in opinion polls despite an electorate-wide lack of enthusiasm for the Government.
Thirdly, the Government has a much more favourable profile in the key area of economic management.
Last but not least the ALP no longer has what its supporters call the "St Carmen" factor to insulate it from the full force of the so-called "WA Inc" debacle.

"WA Inc" refers to the former Labor Government's attempt to make the public sector a major player in business through a series of high profile direct investments by several controversial, publicly-owned quangoes.
The investments proved largely unsuccessful and a major drain on the public purse and today the Party considers itself lucky to have lost "only" six seats in 1993.
Insiders credit the then leader, Carmen Lawrence, with saving Labor from an even more massive defeat.
"The electorate loved Carmen," said one senior Labor source. "I think Carmen was worth 12 seats to us. All things considered I think it will be very difficult for us to advance."

On the Government side, the main fear appears to be that it may have to rely on independents - albeit conservative minded - to retain power after the election. This follows a string of defections from the Party both by sitting and would-be MPs.
The most vulnerable Government seats are Bunbury, Yokine, Wanneroo, Joondalup, Ballajura and Innaloo, and all bar Bunbury are in Perth's northern suburbs.
A number have been redrawn as a result of the redistribution and only two (Bunbury and Innaloo) are being defended by sitting members.

In Yokine, the Liberal candidate is the sitting member for Dianella, Kim Hames, who can claim to represent a substantial proportion of the new electorate but he is running against another sitting member, Labor's high profile spokesman on police and small business, Nick Catania.

In Joondalup and Wanneroo the Liberals fear they may face challengers backed by the former Liberal now independent Federal MP, Paul Filing, who has already come out in support of the former Liberal Party member, Peter Kyle, a candidate in the blue-ribbon conservative seat of Carine.

When contacted by Reuters, Filing said he would also support the former Liberal MP now independent upper house member, Reg Davies. "I think independents can bring a different perspective to the business of government," Filing said.
"There have been expressions of interest from other people thinking of running as independents but it would depend on circumstances whether I would back any," he said.
In the Legislative Council 34 members representing six regions are elected by proportional representation.
The three metropolitan regions with almost 820,000 electors return the same number of MPs (17) as the three country regions with a combined enrolment of less than 290,000.

The ALP describes this as "the worst malapportionment in the country" but, ironically, is one of the beneficiaries: its rural stronghold - the Mining and Pastoral Region - with less than 67,000 electors has the same number of MPs as the Agricultural Region with almost 90,000.
Currently the Coalition holds 18 seats and Labor 13 with the remaining three held by two independents (one former Liberal - Davies - and one former Labor, Sam Piantadosi) and the Green Party.

Based on their good showing in the recent Federal election, and despite a bitter split in their ranks, the Democrats are considered a good chance to win a seat in the Council, possibly at the expense of Davies, in the North Metropolitan Region.
The fate of the independent Green, Jim Scott, in South Metropolitan is unclear.
Meanwhile the ALP believes it has a good chance of winning back the North Metropolitan seat it lost to the Liberals last time around because of its failure to lodge a block voting ticket.
It also expects to win back the seat held by Piantodosi, who is running as an independent in the Assembly seat of Yokine.
With the Council already finely balanced, the stage may be set for a 17:17 (Coalition/non-Coalition) seat tie.
